title: I lost the source code to my first game, so I reverse-engineered it with Codex
author: xpsitsme
selftext:
Back in 2015 I made a little Unity puzzle game called **leadball** and released it only on iOS. I don’t remember exactly when I lost the source code, but it was pretty soon after launch.

When I wanted to pick it up again, I used Codex to reverse-engineer my own game. It helped me piece enough of the code back together to get it building in Unity again. That’s where **Kinetile** started.

The idea is still the same. You move tiles around, press Start, and watch where the ball goes. I brought back all 28 original puzzles and added another 28. In some of the new ones, the ball hits a button that makes platforms slide into place. The trick is getting the bridge ready before the ball reaches the gap.

I used Codex and Claude for coding and debugging. Claude was a huge help with Infinity mode, which generates new puzzles right on your device. I used Suno for the music, and AI also helped with sound effects and artwork.

I decided how the game should play, designed and playtested the levels, and chose what to carry over from leadball. One thing I kept checking was where the ball landed after a bounce. Change that a little and a solution from 2015 can suddenly miss the next tile.

I’ve been programming professionally for over 10 years. Even with that experience, I don’t think I’d have finished the version I had in mind on my own without AI.

Kinetile is coming to Steam for Windows and macOS, and to iOS for iPhone and iPad. The [free browser demo on itch.io](https://sochalewski.itch.io/kinetile) has the first 14 levels. If it looks like your kind of puzzle, I’d appreciate a [wishlist on Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5469840/Kinetile/).

Has anyone else here ever had to reverse-engineer their own game? 😂
